title: Correcting the Attribution: de Bruijn–Erdős, Not Sylvester–Gallai
content: The central conceptual contribution of this entry lives in the docstring. The parent entry recorded 'n non-collinear points determine at least n lines' in prose and labeled it Sylvester–Gallai — but that is a *different* theorem (Sylvester–Gallai asserts the existence of an ordinary line, one through exactly two points). The 'at least n lines' bound is the de Bruijn–Erdős theorem (1948). The honest-scope note is equally important: the file formalizes only the combinatorial incidence content; the genuinely open questions (Sylvester–Gallai, Green–Tao's ≥ n/2 ordinary lines, the achievable line-count set) need projective-geometry / polynomial-method machinery and are deliberately left open. The setup abstracts away the plane: P and L are arbitrary types with a membership relation, and HasLines supplies the single axiom 'two points determine a unique line'.
mathContext: de Bruijn–Erdős: $n$ points $\Rightarrow \ge n$ lines. Sylvester–Gallai (distinct): $\exists$ a line through exactly two points.
relatedConcepts: honest scoping of a WIP formalization
prerequisites: the distinction between line-count and ordinary-line theorems
Configuration.HasLines as the 'unique line through two points' axiom

title: de Bruijn–Erdős: At Least n Lines
content: deBruijn_erdos states Fintype.card P ≤ Fintype.card L: a finite set of points in which any two determine a unique line gives at least as many lines as points. This is the de Bruijn–Erdős theorem (1948) — the correct attribution for the parent entry's prose claim 'at least n lines', which had been mislabeled Sylvester–Gallai (a different statement about ordinary lines). The proof is a one-liner delegating to Mathlib's Configuration.HasLines.card_le, internally a double-counting argument over point- and line-incidence counts. The hypotheses [HasLines P L] [Fintype P] [Fintype L] are exactly the abstract incidence axioms a finite, not-all-collinear planar point set satisfies.
mathContext: $|P| \le |L|$: $n$ non-collinear points determine at least $n$ distinct lines.

title: Upper Bound C(n,2) by Pair Counting
content: card_le_choose_two proves Fintype.card L ≤ C(|P|,2). Assuming every line passes through at least two points, `choose` extracts for each line l a distinct pair p l ≠ q l on it, defining f : L → Finset P by f l = {p l, q l}. The map is injective: if f l₁ = f l₂ then both lines contain p l₂ and q l₂, and Nondegenerate.eq_or_eq (two points lie on at most one line) forces l₁ = l₂ (the alternative p l₂ = q l₂ is excluded). Since each f l is a 2-element subset (Finset.card_pair), the image lands in the 2-subsets, and the calc chain via Finset.card_image_of_injective and Finset.card_powersetCard counts |L| ≤ C(n,2). The injectivity rests on the same uniqueness axiom that powers the lower bound.
relatedConcepts: uniqueness of the line through two points

title: The Line-Count Sandwich n ≤ #L ≤ C(n,2)
content: line_count_sandwich packages both bounds as a conjunction: the number of lines determined by n points lies in [n, C(n,2)]. The lower bound is de Bruijn–Erdős (HasLines.card_le), the upper bound the pair-counting injection (card_le_choose_two) — and both rest on the same uniqueness axiom that two points determine at most one line. This is the verified combinatorial range underlying Erdős 606; the #print axioms checks at the end of the file confirm only the foundational propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound are used (0 counted axioms). Which intermediate counts in [n, C(n,2)] are actually achievable is the deeper open question.
